How Data Systems Keep Their Promises A database can accept a write while a search index misses it. A retry can count the same purchase twice. A server can appear dead when its network is merely slow. These problems connect the subjects in Martin Kleppmann’s Designing Data-Intensive Applications.
The central argument is that sound architecture requires an understanding of mechanisms, guarantees, and trade-offs. Product names alone tell us little. Engineers need to know what a system promises, what assumptions support that promise, and what happens when those assumptions fail. The author’s introduction presents this comparison of underlying ideas as the book’s purpose.
This summary covers the 2017 first edition, written by Kleppmann alone. Its three parts move from the foundations of data systems to distributed data and then derived data. The examples below simplify the mechanisms to explain their practical consequences.
Start with Reliability, Scalability, and Maintainability Kleppmann gives system design three broad goals. Reliability means continuing to work correctly despite faults. A broken disk is a fault; losing the service’s ability to meet its requirements is a failure. Good design prevents expected faults from becoming failures.
Scalability concerns how a system handles growth. First describe the load. Requests per second, data volume, and the distribution of activity can expose different limits. Then measure performance under that load. An average response time can hide the slow requests that cause users difficulty.
Maintainability includes operating the system, understanding it, and changing it. A design that needs constant expert intervention has a real cost, even if its benchmark looks good. These goals, developed in the opening chapter, make operational work part of architecture.
Choose Data Models Around Relationships The book compares relational, document, and graph models. Each makes some relationships easier to express.
A document can keep a self-contained record together. A relational model can represent shared entities without copying their details everywhere. A graph model makes connections central to queries. Consider a professional network: a profile, its employment history, and paths between connected people present different modeling needs.
The question is how the data will be read and changed. Duplicating an organization name inside many records may simplify a read. Renaming that organization then requires many updates. Normalization reduces this duplication but can require joins.
Declarative query languages add another useful separation. The application states the result it needs, while the database chooses an execution plan. Kleppmann’s data-model discussion encourages readers to examine these consequences before choosing a database family.
Storage Engines Move Costs Between Operations An index speeds up selected reads by maintaining an additional structure. That structure consumes space and adds work to writes. Every index therefore supports some access patterns at a cost.
Kleppmann compares B-trees with log-structured storage, including LSM-trees. B-trees organize data in pages and update those pages. LSM-based designs buffer writes and merge sorted data files over time. Their background merging, called compaction, creates additional work. Neither structure wins for every workload.
The distinction between transactions and analytics is equally important. Looking up one order differs from calculating sales across a large history. Column-oriented storage can help analytical scans by reading the relevant columns and compressing similar values together. The storage chapter connects internal structures to these workload choices. Its practical lesson is to investigate the work an engine performs, then measure it with representative data.
Design for Old and New Software to Coexist Data often outlives the code that created it. During a rolling deployment, old and new services may run together. Stored records may remain for years.
Kleppmann examines encoding formats and schema evolution through compatibility. Backward compatibility lets new code read old data. Forward compatibility lets old code read data produced by new code, within defined limits. Adding an optional field with a sensible default can be easier than changing the meaning of an existing field.
A database that does not enforce a schema still has expectations in application code. Those expectations need management. The encoding and evolution chapter treats compatibility as a requirement across databases, service calls, and messages.
Replication and Partitioning Solve Different Problems Replication keeps copies of the same data on several machines. It can improve availability, reduce geographic distance, and increase read capacity. Its difficult part is coordinating changes.
With asynchronous leader-based replication, a leader can acknowledge a write before a follower receives it. A user who updates a profile and then reads from that follower may see the old profile. Reading one’s own writes is a specific guarantee that addresses this experience. Synchronous replication waits for acknowledgment from participating replicas, adding delay and dependence on their availability. Multi-leader and leaderless approaches introduce further questions about conflicting writes. These trade-offs are developed in the replication chapter.
Partitioning, also called sharding, divides a dataset into pieces. Different machines can store and process different pieces. Range partitioning preserves useful ordering but can concentrate traffic. Hash partitioning can spread keys more evenly, while making range queries harder. A single popular key can still create a hot spot.
Replication and partitioning often work together: each partition has several replicas. The extra capacity comes with routing, rebalancing, and cross-partition coordination costs, as the partitioning chapter explains.
Transactions Define What Concurrent Work Can Observe Transactions help applications handle partial updates and concurrent access. However, the label “ACID” does not fully specify behavior. Isolation levels differ, and their names can hide differences between implementations.
Consider two people editing the same record. Both read its original value, then each writes a replacement. Without suitable protection, one change can overwrite the other. Other anomalies involve transactions that update different records while jointly breaking a rule.
Serializability means committed transactions have an effect equivalent to running them one at a time in some order. Systems can achieve it through serial execution, locking, or techniques that detect conflicts and abort transactions. Applications must handle retries correctly. Kleppmann’s transaction chapter and his Hermitage isolation tests support a precise approach: name the anomaly that must be prevented, then verify the chosen guarantee.
Distributed Systems Must Act Under Uncertainty A timeout cannot tell us exactly what happened. A request may have been lost. The server may have completed it and lost the reply. The server may still be working.
Clocks can disagree, processes can pause, and networks can delay messages. These are normal design conditions in the distributed-systems discussion. Treating a timeout as proof that an operation failed can make a retry unsafe.
The next step is to define stronger abstractions. Linearizability makes operations appear to act on one current copy of the data, respecting real-time order. It differs from serializability, which concerns transactions and their possible serial order.
Consensus allows nodes to agree on decisions, such as an ordered sequence of operations. It supports coordination despite failures, under stated assumptions. It cannot promise progress through every loss of communication. The consistency and consensus chapter explains the value and cost of these guarantees.
Kleppmann also rejects using CAP as a vague “pick two” slogan. During a network partition, linearizability conflicts with the theorem’s requirement that every request to a non-failing node receive a successful response. His CAP explanation shows why actual operations and configurations need closer examination.
Derived Data Connects Databases, Batches, and Streams An application may need a database, a search index, and an analytical store. Kleppmann distinguishes authoritative records from derived data, which can be reconstructed from other data.
Batch processing transforms a bounded input into an output. Its predictable inputs make reprocessing useful: correct a transformation and rebuild the result. Stream processing handles events that continue arriving. It must also account for late events, ordering, and recovery.
Logs connect these ideas. A retained sequence of changes can feed multiple consumers. Change data capture exposes database changes so other systems can maintain derived views. This avoids relying on an application to make two independent writes succeed together. The author’s related report, Making Sense of Stream Processing, explains this integration model.
Recovery still requires care. Replaying an event must not apply a business effect twice. An idempotent operation has the same effect when repeated. Deduplication and atomic updates can also help, within their supported boundaries. The stream-processing chapter makes fault tolerance part of data processing rather than an afterthought.
Practical Implications and Limits My practical reading is to begin a design review with promises: which records are authoritative, how stale a read may be, which rules must always hold, and what a retry can repeat. Then ask how the team will detect errors and rebuild damaged results. These questions turn broad goals into testable requirements.
The book’s final chapter also examines privacy, tracking, and predictive analytics. Technical correctness does not settle whether collecting or using data serves people well. Kleppmann explicitly presents his future-system proposals as opinions for discussion.
The book provides conceptual depth rather than deployment instructions. Its first-edition product examples describe their period; they should not establish the capabilities of a current release. Readers must check current documentation and test their own configurations. Understanding the theory also does not remove the need for backups, monitoring, recovery practice, or judgment about operational complexity.
Its lasting contribution is a method of asking better questions. A useful architecture makes its assumptions visible and chooses guarantees that fit the consequences of being wrong.
Sources Martin Kleppmann: first-edition publication record and purpose. O’Reilly: first-edition title, author, and contents, with chapter previews linked throughout this summary. Kleppmann: Hermitage transaction-isolation tests, a supporting explanation of isolation differences. Kleppmann: CAP and linearizability, a supporting technical explanation. Kleppmann: Making Sense of Stream Processing, a separate, related report on logs and data integration.

Building Software Requires More Than Adding People A software project falls behind. Management assigns more programmers. The deadline moves further away. Frederick P. Brooks Jr. explains why this response can fail in The Mythical Man-Month: Essays on Software Engineering.
His broader argument concerns the cost of dividing intellectual work. A large system needs many contributors, but users need one coherent product. Organizing the work must preserve that unity while allowing people to build different parts.
Brooks draws on his experience managing IBM’s System/360 and OS/360 projects. The original collection appeared in 1975. This summary also covers the 1995 anniversary edition, which retains the earlier essays and adds later reflections, including “No Silver Bullet.” Those additions matter because Brooks changes some of his advice. The publisher’s edition description explains this structure.
Effort and Calendar Time Are Different A person-month measures effort: one person’s work over one month. It does not establish how quickly a team can finish a project. The same total effort can produce different completion dates.
Brooks distinguishes work that people can divide freely from work that requires coordination or a fixed sequence. Software often contains both constraints. A team cannot test an interaction before the relevant parts exist. Splitting a feature also creates boundaries that people must define and maintain.
New staff add two costs. They need training from people who already understand the system. They also increase the communication needed to keep the work aligned. Reassigning tasks takes effort too. Under deadline pressure, these costs can exceed the extra capacity.
This is the mechanism behind Brooks’s law: adding people to an already late software project can make it later. His essay on the man-month challenges the assumption that effort converts directly into progress.
For an illustrative example, imagine a team repairing a payment system. New engineers may help with a separate reporting task. They may initially slow repairs to a tangled transaction engine because its current experts must explain the design and review unfamiliar changes. The useful question is which remaining tasks newcomers can safely take over.
Recover a Schedule by Changing the Plan Brooks’s warning does not mean a team must remain understaffed forever. It means that late hiring is a project change with costs, rather than an immediate cure.
In a later interview about the book, Brooks identifies several responses to delay: set a credible new schedule, reduce the promised work, or release essential functions first and deliver others later. Each response changes an actual constraint.
My practical reading is to review the remaining dependencies before changing headcount. Identify what must happen in sequence. Ask what requires scarce expert attention. Then decide whether extra staff will remove a bottleneck or place more demands on it.
For example, postponing a custom reporting feature may let a team finish a reliable core service. Merely asking everyone to work faster leaves the original planning error unresolved.
Give the Product One Coherent Design Conceptual integrity means that a system’s parts follow a consistent set of ideas. Users can learn a rule in one place and apply it elsewhere. They do not need to reconstruct the history of the teams that built each feature.
Brooks treats this unity as more valuable than collecting every attractive feature. He favors one architect, or a small group that agrees on the design, to control the system’s external concepts. Many people can implement those concepts without each inventing a different product. The system-design essay introduces this concern through the unity of a cathedral’s architecture.
Consider an illustrative document service. If deleting, sharing, and restoring a file follow consistent rules across the service, users can predict the results. If each department defines those actions differently, extra features may increase confusion.
A useful application is to document the few promises that must hold everywhere. Who can change access? What does deletion mean? Which failures can users recover from? These decisions give implementation teams a common boundary while leaving room for invention within it.
Organize Support Around Skilled Design Work Brooks explores a surgical team, developing an organizational proposal associated with Harlan Mills. A chief programmer leads the central design and implementation. Other roles provide design support, testing, tools, documentation, and administration.
The aim is to scale useful work without making every contributor negotiate every central decision. Brooks’s team essay begins with the tension between a small skilled group and a large project’s demands.
The lasting question is how to protect difficult technical work from avoidable interruption. A team may gain more from better test tools or clear documentation than from assigning another person to the same code.
My caution is that concentrating knowledge also creates a risk. If only one person understands a critical component, the team becomes fragile. Applying Brooks’s principle requires shared understanding and review alongside clear responsibility. His period-specific staffing model need not become a literal organization chart.
Success Can Encourage Too Much Design The second-system effect describes a temptation after an initial success. A designer puts deferred ideas into the next system. Confidence grows, restraint weakens, and the replacement becomes overloaded.
Brooks also warns against perfecting techniques whose original purpose has disappeared. A successful old approach can consume attention even when changed conditions call for another design. His second-system essay stresses communication between architects and builders about cost and feasibility.
An illustrative replacement for a simple booking tool might acquire elaborate scheduling rules, custom dashboards, and many optional workflows. Each addition seems reasonable. Together they can obscure the basic task of making a booking.
The practical discipline is to give features a cost and a purpose. Ask which user problem each feature solves and how much complexity it adds. Experience should improve selection, rather than become permission to include everything.
Measure Finished Behavior and Test the Connections Brooks explains that serious delay can accumulate through small daily slips. Each looks manageable until the total becomes impossible to hide. His essay on schedule failure makes this gradual loss of time central.
Clear milestones help expose it. A milestone should identify a specific result, rather than a hopeful impression of progress. Managers also need conditions in which people can report trouble without automatically losing control of their work.
For example, “the import feature is nearly finished” gives little evidence. “The service imports the agreed sample, rejects invalid records, and passes its acceptance checks” gives people something concrete to inspect. This is an application of the principle, not a milestone from the book.
Brooks also separates working components from a working whole. His integration and testing essay asks how tested programs become a dependable system. Parts may work separately while disagreeing about data or behavior. In a booking service, a successful reservation screen proves little if the inventory service still allows the same room to be sold twice.
Plan for Learning, Then Build in Increments The original book advises planning to discard an initial system because development reveals what the first design missed. Read alone, this can sound like a recommendation to build an entire product twice.
The anniversary edition revisits that advice. Brooks rejects a one-pass development model and favors growing a working system through increments. The publisher’s sample contents explicitly identifies this correction in the retrospective chapter.
The distinction is useful. A prototype can answer a narrow question without becoming the foundation of the final service. An incremental product can then add tested capabilities while preserving useful work.
For an illustrative booking system, first test whether users understand room availability. Then build a minimal working reservation path. Add cancellation and other functions as the team learns. The aim is to discover errors while changes remain manageable.
Better Tools Do Not Remove Every Hard Decision In “No Silver Bullet”, Brooks separates essential difficulty from accidental difficulty. Essential work concerns the problem’s concepts and relationships. Accidental work comes from representing those concepts with particular tools and machines.
He identifies complexity, conformity to outside rules, changeability, and invisibility as sources of difficulty. Software has many interacting states. It must fit existing institutions. People keep requesting changes. Its structure is hard to see as a whole.
His claim was specific: no single technical or management advance promised a tenfold improvement within the following decade. He still expected progress through combined improvements, reuse, prototypes, incremental growth, and better designers.
My interpretation is to evaluate a tool by the difficulty it removes. Faster implementation can help greatly. It does not by itself decide which access rules a hospital needs or resolve conflicting definitions of a valid payment.
Use the Book as a Guide to Judgment These essays offer experience-based arguments, not universal equations. Brooks’s later preface acknowledges how few original propositions had received decisive research tests. Historical staffing and computing arrangements also limit literal application.
The most useful lesson is to examine the structure of the work. Before increasing staff or promises, inspect dependencies, design consistency, testing, and the team’s ability to learn. A credible plan accounts for those activities as part of building software.
Sources Addison-Wesley / InformIT: anniversary edition, author credit, and overview. Publisher’s sample: copyright record, prefaces, and detailed contents. O’Reilly: book contents and legitimate chapter previews, with individual essays linked above. Brooks: “No Silver Bullet,” UNC technical report, 1986. Brooks interview: “Quoted Often, Followed Rarely,” Fortune, 2005; reproduced by Calvin University.

The People Behind a Working Computer A computer can look like an impersonal object. Tracy Kidder makes its creation intensely personal. The Soul of a New Machine, first published in 1981, follows engineers at Data General as they develop a computer called Eagle. The machine reached the market as the Eclipse MV/8000.
Kidder writes narrative nonfiction rather than a design manual. His subject is the work of building: choosing compromises, accepting responsibility, finding faults, and keeping a team together. He shows how people can give extraordinary effort to a project that offers them both creative freedom and exhaustion. The publisher’s description confirms the book’s focus on the culture of computer development.
There is no simple rule that explains the team’s success. My reading of the central idea is that technology carries the choices of its makers. A working machine emerges from technical skill, personal ambition, negotiation, and institutional pressure. The title’s “soul” is best treated as an invitation to examine those human commitments, rather than a precise technical claim.
A New Machine Must Fit an Existing World The story takes place in the late 1970s. Digital Equipment Corporation’s VAX threatens Data General’s position in minicomputers. These were business and scientific systems, often housed in cabinets. “Mini” distinguished them from larger computers; it did not mean a modern pocket device.
Data General has a major development effort in North Carolina. Tom West leads a group in Massachusetts that pursues Eagle as another route. The two efforts compete within the same company. Eagle must therefore survive an internal struggle for attention and resources while addressing an external competitor.
Its central constraint is compatibility. Customers have already invested in software for Data General’s Eclipse machines. Eagle should offer a path to greater capability without making that investment worthless. Historian Thomas Haigh’s retrospective explains the project’s combination of old instruction compatibility and a new 32-bit architecture.
For a general reader, the important point is the migration problem. Imagine replacing a workshop’s machinery while keeping its existing tools usable. A fresh design might be elegant in isolation. A compatible design must also respect work that people have already done. That requirement can make an apparently untidy solution valuable.
This is an application of the story, not a universal preference for old systems. Compatibility has costs too. The question is which changes customers can absorb and which changes would force them to start again.
Engineering Includes Choosing What to Leave Out West’s job involves more than finding the most advanced design. He must get a useful product finished. His standards concern the machine’s cost, performance, schedule, and place in the business.
In a 1982 discussion with Kidder at the Computer Museum, West argues that attempts at perfection can defeat delivery within time and cost limits. Kidder, in turn, describes engineers’ concern for technical beauty. Their exchange helps explain a tension running through the book: craftsmanship and commercial judgment sometimes pull in different directions.
This does not make careless work good engineering. A machine that produces wrong results has failed its basic purpose. The useful distinction is between essential correctness and optional refinement. Teams need judgment about which compromises preserve the product’s purpose.
Consider an illustrative software project. Keeping stored records safe is essential. Reworking an internal naming convention may be less urgent. Both can improve quality, but treating them as equally urgent can prevent a release. The Eagle story encourages readers to ask what a proposed improvement protects, who benefits, and what it delays.
Real Responsibility Makes the Work Compelling The young engineers receive substantial parts of the machine to build. The hardware group becomes known as the Hardy Boys. The microcode group becomes the Microkids. Microcode supplies detailed internal control instructions that connect the machine’s circuits to the operations it must perform.
Kidder calls the team’s commitment signing up. Accepting a task means taking responsibility for seeing it through, including demands that may extend far beyond ordinary working hours. Another team term, pinball, describes a distinctive reward: successful work earns the chance to do another challenging project. These ideas appear in Kidder’s legitimate excerpt, “Flying Upside Down.”
The appeal is easy to understand. A person can point to part of a functioning system and know that their decisions made it work. Responsibility makes learning urgent and success tangible.
My practical interpretation is that meaningful ownership requires a complete piece of work. Merely assigning more tasks is different. A person needs enough context to understand the result and enough authority to influence it. They also need help when the work exceeds their experience.
The difficult question is what happens when identity becomes tied to delivery. If missing a date feels like proving oneself unworthy, a commitment can become hard to revise even after new facts appear. Pride can support persistence while also discouraging honest limits.
Leadership Happens Between the Team and the Company West is a demanding and often distant presence. He also works to secure room for the project within Data General. The reader sees leadership as a mixture of technical judgment, persuasion, protection, and pressure. It is difficult to isolate one trait and declare it the cause of success.
The later WIRED account, based on interviews with participants, revisits the contrast between West’s public severity and his efforts to protect the team. It also shows why a portrait of one project cannot capture an entire person or career.
In the museum discussion, West defends giving engineers difficult questions to solve rather than supplying every answer. This makes autonomy more demanding than simple freedom from supervision. Someone still has to decide when an engineer needs space and when a problem requires intervention.
For a present-day reader, the useful question is what the manager makes possible. Does the team have clear priorities, access to help, and resources? Can members raise a risk without losing respect? These are my review questions, not a management checklist offered by Kidder.
A leader’s visible manner can distract from these conditions. Copying a successful manager’s bluntness may reproduce the discomfort without reproducing the judgment or support that made the work possible.
A Prototype Is the Start of Another Hard Problem Designing the parts does not establish that they work together. Debugging becomes a major part of the story. Engineers must turn a failure into evidence, then trace that evidence to its cause.
In “The Ultimate Toy,” Kidder follows a fault involving inconsistent copies of instructions in the machine’s memory system. The visible failure occurs after the underlying mistake. The engineers must reconstruct what happened earlier instead of assuming that the final symptom identifies the cause.
A simple analogy is a worker following an outdated instruction sheet. The wrong action may occur long after somebody failed to replace the sheet. Watching the action alone does not explain where the process broke.
This illustrates why integration needs its own time and tools. Separate parts can appear sound while their interaction fails. A schedule that ends when components are assembled leaves out the work of establishing dependable behavior.
The broader application is to preserve evidence. A reproducible failure, a careful record, and a specific hypothesis can help more than another confident guess. Persistence matters, but useful persistence changes what the team knows.
Finishing Changes the Meaning of the Work Eagle becomes a product, but completion does not preserve the team’s shared world. The project that organized people’s days and gave their effort meaning cannot remain a permanent emergency. Kidder’s ending contains loss as well as achievement.
Haigh emphasizes this shift in his retrospective. The underdog success does not resolve every personal or organizational tension. That makes the ending central to the book’s meaning. A company’s successful product and an engineer’s satisfying life are related outcomes, but they are not identical.
My interpretation is that finishing deserves preparation too. Recognition, rest, and a credible next assignment matter because people have invested more than hours. Treating completion only as a transfer to sales or operations can overlook what the builders must leave behind.
Read the Achievement with Its Costs in View This is one closely observed project, not a controlled comparison of management methods. It cannot prove that harsh schedules, internal rivalry, or a distant leader caused success. The machine’s completion does not tell us which burdens were necessary and which could have been avoided.
The social setting also limits generalization. The central engineering culture is heavily male. A model of commitment that assumes people can surrender evenings and weekends fits some lives more easily than others. Readers should examine whom such a model excludes before treating it as a hiring standard.
Even the observation has limits. In their museum discussion, West and Kidder acknowledge that the writer’s presence changed the situation he was recording. Access provides insight without making the account a neutral measurement.
The book remains useful because it holds admiration and discomfort together. Difficult work can offer deep pleasure. Organizations can benefit from that pleasure while asking too much of the people who feel it. A thoughtful application preserves ownership, technical curiosity, and careful investigation while questioning the assumption that devotion requires unlimited sacrifice.
Sources Hachette Book Group: title, sole author credit, publication history, and overview. Tracy Kidder: “Flying Upside Down,” The Atlantic, July 1981, an authorized book excerpt. Tracy Kidder: “The Ultimate Toy,” The Atlantic, August 1981, an authorized excerpt about debugging. Tracy Kidder and Tom West: Computer Museum discussion, October 17, 1982, printed in the Spring 1983 report; the discussion starts on PDF page 30. Thomas Haigh: “The Immortal Soul of an Old Machine,” Communications of the ACM, January 2021, a historical interpretation used for context and limitations. Evan Ratliff: “O, Engineers!”, WIRED, 2000, a later account with participant interviews.
